newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines to step up reforms pace in '97.
newsitem.headline: Philippines to step up reforms pace in '97.

text.p: The Philippines, which recorded its highest growth in the past nine years in 1996, will step up its reforms programme this year to sustain expansion of the economy, Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo said on Thursday.
"For this year, we will not be lulled into complacency by the bright economic picture that prevails today," de Ocampo told bankers at a forum.
"The Philippines has finally managed to take that proverbial economic take-off. We have changed our image from being the proverbial sick man of Asia to the newest tiger, the fast rising star."

Despite Gross National Product (GNP) growth of more than seven percent in the first three quarters of 1996 and a forecast 7.1 percent for the full year, the highest level since 1987, the government is aware that improving its fiscal position should be a top priority, he said.

De Ocampo said the foremost priorities were to provide a sustainable source of revenue for the government by putting in place the remaining components of a comprehensive tax reform package and increasing the savings rate.
After nearly a year of political wrangling, the government last November managed to approve beer and cigarette taxes, the most controversial part of the tax reform package.
The new method of computing "sin taxes" was expected to bring in additional annual revenue of about 6.5 billion pesos ($250 million).

Last year, the Philippines' fiscal position was strong with the government reporting a 10.65 billion peso ($400 million) budget surplus for the first 11 months. But economists said the true situation was not really comfortable.

In a country report issued last August, the Asian Development Bank said privatisation of state assets had brought in large sums of money but "the unsustainability of this source of revenue in the long run points to an underlying fragility of the fiscal balance."
The remaining parts of the tax reform package deal with personal and corporate taxes.
"Our tax effort reached 16.3 percent (of GNP) during the first 11 months of 1996 ... but this is still below the 18 percent ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) average," de Ocampo said.
The government also hopes to cut costs by privatising services, he said.
De Ocampo said another priority would be attracting higher investments into the country, adding: "We will push for the implementation of what we call the Hongkongisation programme."
The term comes from the hope that many businesses would leave Hong Kong after the colony's handover to China at the end of June and relocate to Manila.
The Philippines would change several laws this year to make foreign investments in the country easier, de Ocampo said.
